anchor: The rain set early in to-night
title: Publication and 'Madhouse Cells'
short: First printed as 'Porphyria' (Monthly Repository, Jan. 1836); paired with 'Johannes Agricola' as 'Madhouse Cells' in Dramatic Lyrics (1842); titled 'Porphyria's Lover' in 1863.
body: This is Browning's earliest short dramatic monologue and his first study of a disordered mind. It appeared, signed 'Z', in W. J. Fox's Monthly Repository in January 1836. In Dramatic Lyrics (1842) Browning placed it beside 'Johannes Agricola in Meditation' under the joint title 'Madhouse Cells', which told readers that the speaker is insane; the present title dates from the 1863 collected Poetical Works, where the label was dropped (the archive's heading cites the later 1845 volume). Removing the frame shifts the burden of judgment onto the reader, who must infer madness from the speaker's calm, orderly account.

title: Metre and stanza
short: Sixty lines of iambic tetrameter rhymed ababb, printed without stanza breaks: a tight, obsessive pattern under a calm surface.
body: The poem falls into twelve five-line units rhymed ababb, but they are run together without breaks and the sentences often overrun the units (for example ll. 10-11, 'from her form / Withdrew the dripping cloak'). The doubled b-rhyme gives each unit a heavy close; critics have compared the effect to a mind circling a fixed idea. The regular four-beat line and the plain narrative syntax contrast grimly with the content, making the murder sound like one domestic action among others ('I found / A thing to do').

anchor: The sullen wind was soon awake
title: The storm
short: A personified storm, 'sullen' and spiteful, mirrors the speaker's brooding mood: a pathetic fallacy that hints at violence to come.
body: The wind tears down the elm-tops 'for spite' and does 'its worst to vex the lake', attributing malice to nature. Ruskin would name this attribution of human feeling to nature the 'pathetic fallacy' in Modern Painters III (1856). Here it serves the dramatic monologue: we see the weather through the speaker's resentful mood, before he tells us that he sat 'with heart fit to break'. Porphyria brings warmth and light into this setting ('Blaze up, and all the cottage warm'), which makes her the active and the speaker the passive figure until the murder.

sources.cite: Daniel Karlin, ed., Robert Browning: Selected Poems (Penguin, 2004), notes to the poem

title: Porphyria
short: The name derives from Greek for 'purple', the colour of royalty and rank, which suits a woman socially above her lover.
body: Purple (Greek porphyra, the costly dye from the murex shellfish) was the colour of imperial and aristocratic dress; Byzantine princes were 'porphyrogenitus', born in the purple. The name thus marks Porphyria's higher social standing, which the poem implies when it speaks of her 'pride, and vainer ties' and of the 'gay feast' she has left. Some critics have connected the name with the disease porphyria (Popowich 1999), reading the woman as an embodiment of illness and the killing as the speaker's recovery; this is one interpretation among several, and the poem's own text does not demand it.

title: glided in
short: Porphyria enters silently and gracefully, almost like an apparition; she acts throughout the first half while the speaker is passive.
body: The inversion ('glided in Porphyria') delays her name to the end of the clause and gives her entrance a dreamlike quality. She then performs a sequence of practical acts: she shuts out the storm, kneels to light the fire, removes her wet cloak and shawl, unties her hat and lets down her hair. Critics note that the speaker records each act with obsessive precision, and that he does not respond when she calls him (l. 15). The sexual frankness of her undressing and her initiative in embracing him unsettled Victorian conventions of female modesty.

sources.cite: Daniel Karlin, ed., Robert Browning: Selected Poems (Penguin, 2004), notes to the poem
Catherine Ross, 'Browning's Porphyria's Lover', The Explicator 60.2 (2002), 68-72

title: soiled gloves
short: Literally gloves dirtied by the storm; some critics read them as a sign of social or sexual compromise in the speaker's eyes.
body: On the literal level Porphyria's gloves are muddied from her walk through 'wind and rain'. Because gloves were a mark of a lady's propriety, critics have taken the detail as part of the speaker's covert judgment of her as sullied or as stepping down to him; Ross reads it, with the hair and the 'rosy little head', as part of the poem's sexual subtext. The speaker's later insistence that, at the moment of murder, she was 'Perfectly pure and good' suggests a need to fix her in a purity he otherwise doubts.

sources.cite: Catherine Ross, 'Browning's Porphyria's Lover', The Explicator 60.2 (2002), 68-72

title: vainer ties dissever
short: 'Dissever' means to cut apart; Porphyria is too weak to break her 'vainer' (more worldly, emptier) social ties and give herself to him forever.
body: The speaker's account of Porphyria's 'struggling passion' implies a social barrier: her 'pride' and other ties (family, rank, perhaps a suitor) prevent marriage. 'Vainer' means more empty or worthless, as the speaker judges them; 'dissever' is a rather literary word for 'sever' (OED). The syntax of ll. 21-25 ('she / Too weak ... ') is the speaker's interpretation, not her words; the poem never lets us hear Porphyria directly, a point emphasised in feminist readings of the monologue.

title: one so pale
short: The speaker himself, pale from pining for love; some critics take the pallor as illness, others as the conventional pallor of the lovesick.
body: Porphyria has left a 'gay feast' because of 'A sudden thought' of her lover, pale with unrequited love. The lovesick lover's pallor is a commonplace of Petrarchan and Romantic convention. Critics who stress the speaker's passivity have read the line as evidence of illness, invalidism or impotence, explaining his inertia in the first half and his violent seizing of control; the Wikipedia summary of criticism records this line of interpretation, but it remains inference from scant evidence.

title: Porphyria worshipped me
short: The speaker's discovery of her love becomes a moment of triumph: his vanity, not her devotion, drives what follows.
body: The speaker looks up at her eyes and concludes 'at last I knew / Porphyria worshipped me'. The religious verb anticipates the poem's final reference to God and shows the speaker placing himself in the position of a deity. His 'surprise / Made my heart swell' and he 'debated what to do': the murder is presented as a deliberate response to a moment of gratified self-esteem. Langbaum's influential account of the dramatic monologue argues that such poems hold us between sympathy and judgment; we enter the speaker's logic even as we recoil from it.

sources.cite: Robert Langbaum, The Poetry of Experience: The Dramatic Monologue in Modern Literary Tradition (1957), ch. 2
Daniel Karlin, ed., Robert Browning: Selected Poems (Penguin, 2004), notes to the poem

title: The preserved moment
short: He kills her to fix for ever a moment in which she is wholly his and perfect: love turned into possession.
body: 'That moment she was mine, mine, fair, / Perfectly pure and good' gives the speaker's motive: the wish to arrest time at its point of perfection. The desire to make a moment eternal recurs in Browning ('The Last Ride Together', 'My Last Duchess', where the Duke prefers his wife as a painting). Critics compare the result to a tableau vivant or a work of art: the living woman is turned into a fixed image. The repeated 'mine, mine' exposes the possessive logic beneath the romantic language.

title: A thing to do
short: The murder is narrated with terrible flatness, as though it were a simple domestic task, which exposes the speaker's detachment.
body: The banal phrase 'I found / A thing to do' leads into the strangling, delayed across the rhyme: her hair 'In one long yellow string I wound / Three times her little throat around, / And strangled her.' The thrice-wound hair has a ritual or magical air. The plainness of the verb 'strangled', placed at the start of a line after the build-up of rhyme, gives a shock. Using her own hair, earlier spread over him as a sign of intimacy, turns the token of love into a weapon, a detail critics read as fetishistic.

title: Sources: Wilson and Procter
short: Possible sources include John Wilson's 'Extracts from Gosschen's Diary' (Blackwood's, 1818) and Bryan Procter's 'Marcian Colonna' (1820).
body: Editors note two Romantic-period sources. John Wilson's 'Extracts from Gosschen's Diary', in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine (1818), is a lurid account of a murder, usually named as a possible source for the poem. Bryan Waller Procter ('Barry Cornwall'), a friend of Browning, acknowledged basing 'Marcian Colonna' (1820) on it, adding the detail of the killer sitting up all night with his victim. Browning's originality lies in giving the murderer his own voice without authorial comment; the influence of Wilson is generally treated as probable rather than proved.

anchor: quite sure she felt no pain
title: Unreliable narration
short: The insistent repetition ('No pain felt she; / I am quite sure') betrays doubt and self-justification: a classic sign of the unreliable speaker.
body: The speaker states the same claim twice in successive lines, the second time with an emphatic 'quite sure'. Such over-assurance is how the dramatic monologue lets readers see more than the speaker does. Ross observes that the speaker's 'romantic egotism' leads him to assume Porphyria's feelings throughout, even after death, culminating in his belief that her head is 'glad' to have its 'utmost will'.

sources.cite: Catherine Ross, 'Browning's Porphyria's Lover', The Explicator 60.2 (2002), 68-72

title: As a shut bud that holds a bee
short: He opens her eyelids cautiously, as one might open a flower bud that might contain a stinging bee: a strange, delicate simile for a grotesque act.
body: 'Warily' and the image of the bee suggest that the speaker half fears what he will find, a living reproach in her eyes. 'Oped' is an archaic form of 'opened'. The natural image of a closed bud recalls Romantic flower-imagery of virginity and innocence, now attached to a corpse. The next line, 'Laughed the blue eyes without a stain', projects happiness onto the dead eyes; 'without a stain' recalls his wish that she be 'pure', and may also hint, grimly, that the strangling has left no visible mark.

sources.cite: Daniel Karlin, ed., Robert Browning: Selected Poems (Penguin, 2004), notes to the poem

anchor: Blushed bright beneath my burning kiss
title: Blushed bright
short: As blood returns when the hair is loosened, her cheek flushes; the speaker reads this physiological effect as a lover's blush.
body: Loosening the tress from her neck allows blood to return to the face, producing colour that the speaker interprets as a response to his kiss. The alliteration on b ('Blushed bright beneath my burning') gives a heightened, quasi-erotic tone to a necrophiliac scene. Here and in 'The smiling rosy little head' (l. 52), Browning lets us see the gap between the physical facts and the speaker's interpretation of them.

sources.cite: Daniel Karlin, ed., Robert Browning: Selected Poems (Penguin, 2004), notes to the poem
Catherine Ross, 'Browning's Porphyria's Lover', The Explicator 60.2 (2002), 68-72

title: Her utmost will
short: He claims her dead head is glad: it has got its deepest wish, to be with him, freed from all that it 'scorned'.
body: The tense shifts to the present ('droops upon it still', 'has its utmost will'), revealing that the speaker is narrating while still sitting with the body. He reinterprets the murder as fulfilment of Porphyria's 'darling one wish', to give herself to him forever (l. 25), and imagines that everything she 'scorned' (the social ties) 'is fled'. The reversal of positions, her head now on his shoulder where his was on hers (ll. 19, 49-50), completes his assertion of control.

sources.cite: Daniel Karlin, ed., Robert Browning: Selected Poems (Penguin, 2004), notes to the poem
Robert Langbaum, The Poetry of Experience: The Dramatic Monologue in Modern Literary Tradition (1957), ch. 2

anchor: God has not said a word
title: God has not said a word
short: The famous last line is variously read as triumph (God approves), unease (he awaits judgment), or a statement of divine silence.
body: Critics divide over the final line. On one reading, the speaker takes God's silence as approval, completing his self-justification; on another, the 'yet' betrays anxiety, as if he is waiting for punishment; a third reading sees Browning raising the problem of a God who does not intervene in human evil. The pairing with 'Johannes Agricola', an antinomian who believes himself saved whatever he does, supports a reading that the speaker presumes divine sanction. The night-long vigil echoes Procter's 'Marcian Colonna'.
